\chapter{Fueron --- They Were, and They Went}
\label{ch:fueron}
\hlchaptermodality{203}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the one plural past that serves both ser and ir.}

I can use the one plural past that serves both ser and ir.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[fueron]{fueron}

\label{lesson:ES-C55-fueron}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Fui} — how many verbs does it belong to? (\textbf{Two}: \emph{ser} and \emph{ir}.) So \emph{fui} is both \emph{I was} and \emph{I went}.

The plural keeps that bargain, and breaks a different one.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the form that refuses the ending}]
\begin{quote}
\emph{\textbf{fueron}} — they were \textbf{and} they went
\end{quote}

Every other past plural you have takes \emph{-aron} or \emph{-ieron}. This one takes neither:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{tener} & \emph{tuv-} + \emph{-ieron} $\to$ \emph{tuvieron} \\
\emph{ser} / \emph{ir} & — $\to$ \textbf{fueron} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Not \emph{fuieron}. The stem simply becomes \emph{fue-} and the \emph{-ron} is stuck on. And \emph{fuimos} is \emph{we were} and \emph{we went}, with the same double duty.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Spanish borrowed its whole past for \emph{to be} from a different verb.}

Latin \textbf{fuī} and \textbf{fuērunt} are the past of a root meaning \emph{to grow}, \emph{to become} — not of \emph{esse}, \emph{to be}. When a verb is used constantly its past tends to wear away, and languages patch the hole from whatever is nearby.

English did exactly the same thing. \emph{Was} and \emph{were} do not come from \emph{be} either; they come from a root meaning \emph{to dwell, to remain}. Two languages, the same hole, the same repair.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{fui · fuimos · fueron}
  \item \emph{fueron} — meaning they were, then meaning they went
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which two verbs does \emph{fueron} serve? (\emph{\textbf{Ser}} and \emph{\textbf{ir}}.)

And why is the past of \emph{to be} built from another verb entirely? (Because a constantly used past \textbf{wears away}, and the hole gets patched — in Spanish and in English both.)
\end{tcolorbox}
